notes: A CASH SALE CAN NOW CARRY VAT. Money taken over the counter is one VAT-inclusive figure, and until now a Fund Receipt booked all of it as income — so a VAT-registered business collected VAT at the counter that never reached its VAT return. Tick "VAT-able sale" on a receipt and the VAT inside the amount is backed out and credited to VAT Output, exactly as an invoice has always done: GHS 6,000 received becomes GHS 1,000 VAT and GHS 5,000 income, stated on screen before anything is saved and printed on the receipt. The option only appears if the organisation says it is VAT-registered and an administrator has named the account, so a school's fund receipts never see it. MONEY BANKED NOW REACHES THE RECONCILIATION FROM EVERY SCREEN. The lodgement register was filled by Fund Receipts and by nothing else, while the reconciliation screen said in as many words that it fills itself. Settling an invoice — the main way a trading business banks money — recorded nothing, and neither did disposal proceeds, cash returned when a petty-cash float is closed, or the receiving side of a bank transfer. Every one of those now enters the register, so the month they were banked no longer reconciles short by their value. CORRECTING A RECEIPT NO LONGER BREAKS THE RECONCILIATION. Correcting a receipt the bank had already credited left a second lodgement for the same deposit that could never be cleared — the bank's own credit line had been used by the first — so every reconciliation from then on carried an uncredited lodgement that did not exist, and the month could not be signed off. And correcting a VAT-able sale when the VAT account had since been unmapped folded the VAT quietly back into income. A CORRECTED CHEQUE NO LONGER REWRITES HISTORY. Keeping the same cheque number on a correction — which the app itself tells you to do — rewrote the date the reconciliation reads. A cheque the bank had ALREADY PAID now keeps the date and the amount it was actually paid for, because those are facts about the bank that our own re-coding does not change; one still outstanding keeps a record of the month it was outstanding in. Either way an already-signed-off month reprints as it was signed off. TAX. Correcting a payment that paid several people no longer re-works each person's withholding from TODAY's rates — what was deducted then is carried through. A withholding certificate and a GRA schedule now print the rate that was ACTUALLY deducted, so reprinting an earlier month after a rate change no longer certifies 7.5% of tax at 5%. Recording a missing cheque against an already-posted VAT remittance refuses a blank number instead of reporting success and writing nothing, and it still works after a later sale has moved the balance. A large Tourism Levy remittance can now be posted at all — it was being held for approval it could never be routed for. BUDGETS AND CORRECTIONS. A back-dated commitment now reserves the budget of its own year rather than this one. The Approval Centre's reversal tool reads the whole ledger instead of the newest 300 vouchers, so an older payroll or remittance voucher — for which it is the only reversal route — can still be reached. A CORRECTION TO WHAT THE LAST RELEASE SAID. Version .62 announced that a backup's checksum is now written into place before the archive it protects. It was not: the change was described but never made, and the gap it was meant to close stayed open for another week. It is done now, and proved by a test. The off-site encrypted copy also chose which old backups to delete by the file's date on disk rather than the date baked into its name — the same mistake the main backup folder was fixed for months ago, left in the one folder that survives the machine, where a cloud client re-dating files could make it delete the newest ledger and keep the oldest. Deleting a company whose books were not on the computer used to CREATE an empty database in their place, which permanently silenced the warning that the books were missing and sent nobody looking for the copy that still existed. HOW THIS RELEASE WAS CHECKED. Thirty independent reviewers went over everything added in the last two releases; twenty-three findings were confirmed and all twenty-three are fixed. Five of the automated guards that are supposed to stop these defects returning turned out not to work — each could be made to pass over the very bug it was written for — and every one has been repaired and then deliberately broken to prove it now fails. A new test drives the installed application through a month of ordinary work — VAT registration, a VAT-able sale, a withheld payment and its cheque — and reads the ledger's own totals back off the screen to check the books balance.
